questions.question_text:
A curve $y = f(x)$ has its only stationary point at $x = 2$.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline f'(x) & -6 & 0 & 5 \end{array}$
What is the nature of the stationary point?

options.why: Read the slope table from right to left, so the negative-to-positive change looked like positive-to-negative.
Used $f'(2) = 0$ on its own and did not compare the signs of $f'$ either side.
Confused a point where $f' = 0$ with a point where only the concavity changes.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(1) = -6 < 0$ and $f'(3) = 5 > 0$
The sign of $f'$ changes from negative to positive, so $x = 2$ is a local minimum.

questions.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = (3 - x)(x + 2)$.
What is the nature of the stationary point at $x = 3$?

options.why: Assumed the larger root of a factorised derivative is always the minimum, as it is for an upward cubic.
Assumed a derivative with two distinct roots gives no sign change at either of them.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(2) = (1)(4) = 4 > 0$
$f'(4) = (-1)(6) = -6 < 0$
The sign of $f'$ changes from positive to negative, so $x = 3$ is a local maximum.

questions.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = -2(x - 5)^{2}$.
What is the nature of the stationary point at $x = 5$?

options.why: Saw the negative coefficient $-2$ and assumed a maximum without testing both sides.
Ignored the factor $-2$, treated $f'$ as positive on both sides, and incorrectly classified a positive-to-positive pattern as a minimum instead of a horizontal point of inflection.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(4) = -2(-1)^{2} = -2 < 0$
$f'(6) = -2(1)^{2} = -2 < 0$
The sign of $f'$ is negative on both sides, so there is no sign change.
$x = 5$ is a horizontal point of inflection.

questions.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $f(x) = xe^{4x}$ and state its nature.

options.why: Correct point, but read the negative-to-positive change in $f'$ as a maximum.
Solved $1 + 4x = 0$ as $x = \tfrac{1}{4}$, dropping the negative sign.
Both dropped the negative sign when solving $1 + 4x = 0$ and reversed the reading of the slope table.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = e^{4x} + 4xe^{4x}$
$= e^{4x}(1 + 4x)$
Since $e^{4x} > 0$, set $1 + 4x = 0$.
$x = -\dfrac{1}{4}$
$f\left(-\tfrac{1}{4}\right) = -\tfrac{1}{4}e^{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{4e}$
$f'(-1) = e^{-4}(-3) < 0$
$f'(0) = 1 > 0$
The sign changes from negative to positive, so $\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}, -\dfrac{1}{4e}\right)$ is a local minimum.

questions.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $f(x) = 4\ln x - x$ for $x > 0$, and state its nature.

options.why: Correct point, but read the positive-to-negative change in $f'$ as a minimum.
Solved $\dfrac{4}{x} = 1$ by inverting the fraction to give $x = \tfrac{1}{4}$.
Inverted $\dfrac{4}{x} = 1$ to get $x = \tfrac{1}{4}$ and also reversed the slope-table reading.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = \dfrac{4}{x} - 1$
Set $f'(x) = 0$:
$\dfrac{4}{x} = 1$
$x = 4$
$f(4) = 4\ln 4 - 4$
$f'(2) = 2 - 1 = 1 > 0$
$f'(8) = \tfrac{1}{2} - 1 = -\tfrac{1}{2} < 0$
The sign changes from positive to negative, so $(4,\ 4\ln 4 - 4)$ is a local maximum.

questions.question_text:
The curve $f(x) = \cos x + \sqrt{3}\,\sin x$ has derivative $f'(x) = -\sin x + \sqrt{3}\cos x$.
At which value of $x$ in $0 \le x \le 2\pi$ does $f$ have a local minimum?

options.why: Took the first solution of $\tan x = \sqrt{3}$ without testing the sign of $f'$ on each side.
Solved $\tan x = \sqrt{3}$ in the second quadrant, using $\pi - \tfrac{\pi}{3}$, where the tangent ratio is negative.
Used $2\pi - \tfrac{\pi}{3}$, the fourth-quadrant reflection, instead of the third-quadrant solution.

questions.solution_text:
Set $f'(x) = 0$:
$\sqrt{3}\cos x = \sin x$
$\tan x = \sqrt{3}$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $x = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$
$f'(\pi) = 0 + \sqrt{3}(-1) = -\sqrt{3} < 0$
$f'\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -(-1) + 0 = 1 > 0$
The sign changes from negative to positive at $x = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$, so that is the local minimum.

questions.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = -3(x + 3)(x - 1)$.
Which statement about its stationary points is correct?

options.text: $f$ has a local minimum at $x = -3$ and a local maximum at $x = 1$.
$f$ has a local maximum at $x = -3$ and a local minimum at $x = 1$.
options.why: Ignored the negative coefficient $-3$, reversing the signs of $f'$ on every interval and hence reversing both classifications.
Found the midpoint of the roots, where the quadratic $f'$ has its maximum, and classified that point as a stationary point of $f$ even though $f'(-1) = 12$.

options.text: $f$ has horizontal points of inflection at $x = -3$ and $x = 1$.
options.why: Used $f' = 0$ at both points without checking the sign changes on either side.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 0$ when $x = -3$ or $x = 1$.
$f'(-4) = -3(-1)(-5) = -15 < 0$
$f'(0) = -3(3)(-1) = 9 > 0$
$f'(2) = -3(5)(1) = -15 < 0$
At $x = -3$ the sign changes from negative to positive, so it is a local minimum.
At $x = 1$ the sign changes from positive to negative, so it is a local maximum.

questions.question_text:
The derivative of $y = f(x)$ is $f'(x) = -6(x + 2)(x - 3)^{2}$.
Which statement correctly classifies its stationary points?

options.text: $x = -2$ is a local maximum, and $x = 3$ is a horizontal point of inflection.
$x = -2$ is a local minimum, and $x = 3$ is a horizontal point of inflection.
options.why: Ignored the negative coefficient $-6$, changing the positive-to-negative pattern at $x = -2$ into negative-to-positive.

options.text: $x = -2$ is a local maximum, and $x = 3$ is a local minimum.
options.why: Assumed the larger stationary $x$-value must be a local minimum without checking that $f'$ remains negative on both sides of $x=3$.

options.text: Both $x = -2$ and $x = 3$ are horizontal points of inflection.
options.why: Assumed the squared factor prevents a sign change at every root, overlooking the sign change of $(x + 2)$ at $x = -2$.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 0$ when $x = -2$ or $x = 3$.
$f'(-3) = -6(-1)(36) = 216 > 0$
$f'(-1) = -6(1)(16) = -96 < 0$
The sign changes from positive to negative at $x = -2$, so it is a local maximum.
$f'(2) = -6(4)(1) = -24 < 0$
$f'(4) = -6(6)(1) = -36 < 0$
The derivative is negative on both sides of $x = 3$, so it is a horizontal point of inflection.

questions.question_text:
The curve $f(x) = x\sqrt{16 - x^{2}}$ has derivative $f'(x) = \dfrac{16 - 2x^{2}}{\sqrt{16 - x^{2}}}$ for $-4 < x < 4$.
What is the $x$-coordinate of the local minimum?

options.why: Found both stationary points but assumed the positive one must be the minimum.
Took the endpoint of the domain instead of solving $16 - 2x^{2} = 0$.
Solved $16 - 2x^{2} = 0$ by multiplying by $2$ to get $x^{2} = 32$ instead of dividing to get $x^{2} = 8$.

questions.solution_text:
Set $16 - 2x^{2} = 0$:
$x^{2} = 8$
$x = \pm 2\sqrt{2}$
The denominator $\sqrt{16 - x^{2}}$ is positive throughout $-4 < x < 4$, so the sign of $f'$ is the sign of $16 - 2x^{2}$.
$f'(-3) = \dfrac{16 - 18}{\sqrt{7}} < 0$
$f'(-2) = \dfrac{16 - 8}{\sqrt{12}} > 0$
The sign changes from negative to positive at $x = -2\sqrt{2}$, so that is the local minimum.
